panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of the dorsal left hand of a 28-year-old man showing asymptomatic hyperpigmentation three days to three weeks after squeezing limes and sun exposure, captioned as phytophotodermatitis; black ovals annotate areas of new pigment. B: Clinical photograph of the dorsal right hand and proximal fingers showing the same lime-associated post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, captioned as phytophotodermatitis with black ovals marking new pigment.
panels.attribution_text: Cohen and Ramsay. Margarita Dermatitis Revisited: A Case Report and Literature Review of Lime-Associated Phytophotodermatitis. Cureus None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Phytophotodermatits on the dorsal hands of a 28-year-old man presenting as asymptomatic hyperpigmentation on both of his hands After slicing and using a machine to squeeze 20 limes on a Saturday morning, a man spent several hours outside on a sunny afternoon. Three days later, on the following Tuesday, the man noted darkening on the dorsal aspect of both his left (A) and right (B) hands. The black ovals surround some of the areas of new pigment on his hands.
in_text_mentions: Photographs of his dorsal hands were taken about three weeks later (Figure 3). They showed hyperpigmentation on the dorsal left and right hands. The skin near some of the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal fingers also demonstrated hyperpigmentation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photo of right forearm showing erythematous patch with bullae after mulberry tree exposure, consistent with phytophotodermatitis. B: Clinical photo of left forearm with new blisters/rash in sun-exposed area, supporting phytophotodermatitis.
panels.attribution_text: Kim and Lee. Severe Phytophotodermatitis Caused by Mulberry Tree: A Case Report and Literature Review.. Archives of plastic surgery 2026. doi:10.1055/a-2699-8042. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical photograph taken before biopsy procedure. Despite conservative treatment, the lesion on the right arm worsened, forming an erythematous patch with bullae ( A ), and the lesion on the left arm also increased in size ( B ). These findings were observed on the fourth day after exposure to the mulberry tree. The lesions were confined to the forearms, correlating with the patient's report of wearing short sleeves and gloves while working outdoors, indicating exposure to sunlight and foliage in these areas. A biopsy was conducted on the bullae located on the right arm.
in_text_mentions: During hospitalization, the lesions on his right forearm showed no signs of improvement, and new blisters accompanied by a rash developed on his left forearm, confined to areas not covered by clothing or gloves ( Fig. 2 ). In light of the lack of progress, an excisional biopsy was performed on the right arm. Further detailed history taking revealed that the patient had been working near a mulberry tree by a utility pole.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real patient's dorsal right hand showing asymptomatic brown pigmented patches; the caption explicitly attributes the dark patches to lime-associated phytophotodermatitis (margarita dermatitis), with acral distribution on thumb, adjacent digits and metacarpophalangeal joints. Black ovals are annotations marking the lesions, not a separate panel.

panels.figure_caption: Asymptomatic pigmented patches are the manifestation of margarita dermatitis on the right hand The black ovals surround several of the dark patches caused by the lime-associated phytophotodermatitis on the man’s dorsal right hand. panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the patient's anterior abdomen at presentation, directly captioned as showing extensive erythema and blistering with a positive Nikolsky sign. The article title and in-text context identify acute phytophotodermatitis; the caption provides the specific manifestation. The atypical designation reflects the article's description of a unique acute reaction and the unusual positive Nikolsky sign.
panels.attribution_text: Agha et al. Unique Acute Phytophotodermatitis Reaction and a Visual Diagnostic Guide.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.59199. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Image of the patient's abdomen at presentation Extensive erythema and blistering with a positive Nikolsky sign on the anterior abdomen.
in_text_mentions: A 48-year-old caucasian female with no past medical history presented to the out-patient dermatology clinic with new onset exquisitely painful, blistering, erythematous skin on her abdomen, chest, neck, and chin that gradually appeared and increased in severity over the course of a three-day period. Physical examination revealed closed vesicles located on her left lower quadrant, overlaying erythematous, tender skin, and a hyperpigmented reaction on her entire anterior chest and abdomen (Figures 1, 2).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a forearm in a case report of fig tree-induced phytophotodermatitis. The caption describes xerotic, erythematous and crusting lesions with subsequent residual hyperpigmentation, and the in-text history links lesions on sun-exposed forearms to picking/pruning fig trees. The panel is a real patient image showing a specific manifestation of phytophotodermatitis.
panels.attribution_text: Pinto et al. Fig Tree-Induced Phytophotodermatitis: A Case Report on the Perils of a Hobby.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.41888. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Skin lesions The affected area exhibits a xerotic appearance, along with erythematous lesions and crusting lesions, which subsequently result in residual hyperpigmentation.
in_text_mentions: t similar episodes with the development of erythematous, mildly painful, and pruritic maculopapular lesions on both upper arms and forearms. These lesions progressed to blisters in the course of 12 hours and resolved with residual hyperpigmentation one week after onset (Figure 1 and Figure 2). There were no other associated signs or symptoms. Contact with drugs, food, or different hygiene or cosmetic products was excluded. The patient mentioned that episodes coincided with sunny days when he was picking figs and pruning a fig tree, recognizing that lesions only developed on exposed body areas.
panels.copyright: Pinto et al. Fig Tree-Induced Phytophotodermatitis: A Case Report on the Perils of a Hobby.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.41888. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real patient showing erythematous, desquamative lesions on the posterior upper arm/forearm, matching the caption. The disease-focused article title (Fig Tree-Induced Phytophotodermatitis) plus the in-text account of lesions restricted to sun-exposed areas after picking figs and pruning a fig tree establishes phytophotodermatitis attribution; the lesion distribution is linear/streaky as expected for this eruption. No vesicles are clearly visible in this panel, so only linear erythema is tagged from the vocabulary, with desquamation/excoriations proposed.

panels.figure_caption: Skin lesions Erythematous and desquamative lesions, in conjunction with scratching abrasions, are visible on the posterior aspect of the patient's upper arm and forearm.
in_text_mentions: t similar episodes with the development of erythematous, mildly painful, and pruritic maculopapular lesions on both upper arms and forearms. These lesions progressed to blisters in the course of 12 hours and resolved with residual hyperpigmentation one week after onset (Figure 1 and Figure 2). There were no other associated signs or symptoms. Contact with drugs, food, or different hygiene or cosmetic products was excluded. The patient mentioned that episodes coincided with sunny days when he was picking figs and pruning a fig tree, recognizing that lesions only developed on exposed body areas.
